name: Shortpay — the margin-recovery agent for staffing suppliers in VMS programs
one_liner: For the controller or VP Finance at a $10M–$100M contract staffing firm that bills through Fieldglass, Beeline or VNDLY, Shortpay is an agent that reads every executed client rate card and every VMS remittance line, flags the lines paid below contract (wrong bill rate, missing OT/shift premium, skipped annual escalation, over-deducted program fee), and files the dispute before the contractual notice window closes.
problem: Contract staffing firms sell hours at a 20–25% gross margin (SIA-cited benchmarks put the US average near 22.7%). The bill rate they get paid is not the rate in their signed agreement: it is whatever the client's VMS has configured. When the rate table in Fieldglass/Beeline is stale, when a shift differential or OT multiplier is not applied, when an annual escalation never gets loaded, or when the MSP fee (typically 3–6% of bill rate) is deducted at the wrong percentage, the remittance comes back a few dollars an hour light. Teambridge's own worked example shows a retroactive $2/hr cut on 20 workers over four weeks wiping out ~37% of that assignment's gross margin, and a 200-contractor book drifting from 22% contracted to 18.5% realized margin. SIA wrote in 2025 that preventable billing errors can cost staffing firms more than 5% of billable revenue annually and that disputes add 7–14 days to DSO. Today the work is done by one or two billing clerks (US average base pay ~$49.8k, per SalaryExpert 2026) eyeballing remittance PDFs against a rate-card spreadsheet, or not done at all — and many supplier agreements waive disputes not raised in writing within a set window (one public contract found requires notice within 30 days of invoice date or the dispute is waived), so unnoticed underpayments become permanent.
target_customer: Controller / VP Finance / back-office director at a US contract staffing firm doing $10M–$100M in revenue (IT, light industrial, healthcare, engineering) where a meaningful share of billings flow through client MSP/VMS programs. They own the billing clerk headcount and the margin number, and they already buy middle-office software (Bullhorn, Avionté, TempWorks) and sometimes contingency recovery audits.
why_now: Three things changed. (1) Document-and-remittance parsing by frontier models is now good enough to read a scanned rate card, an amendment and a consolidated VMS remittance and reconcile them line by line — a16z's Big Ideas 2026 "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) is exactly this bet, and YC's "$15-an-Hour Expert" RFS (Brad Flora, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert) describes the pattern of letting an ordinary back-office person do specialist audit work with an AI behind them. (2) The order-to-cash agent pattern just got a very public proof point: SpaceXSI's five Grok Bots (https://x.ai/news/grok-bot-accounting) took cash reconciliation from 3–4 hours to ~30 minutes and invoicing from 24 hours to minutes, which is the demo every finance back office saw this month. (3) Capital is flowing to staffing AR specifically — Monk raised a $25M Series A in April 2026 (total ~$29M) for staffing invoice submission and collections — which validates the buyer but, per its own public materials, stops at "the client paid less than we invoiced" rather than "the client paid less than the contract says."
comparables: Monk (monk.com, $25M Series A Apr 2026, Footwork/Acrew; ~$29M total) — submits invoices and timesheets to VMS/MSP portals, handles rejections, chases cash, applies payments and flags short-pays; its public staffing materials describe reconciliation to the invoice, not a line-by-line test against the executed rate card and amendments. Hercules.ai (hercules.ai/bill, ~$26M Series B 2024) — the closest functional match: pre-bill checks of invoice lines against contracts, amendments, rate cards, OT multipliers, and reconciliation against VMS self-billing; but it is sold as an operated managed service with no public price, and its showcased customer (Ōnin Group, 18,000+ weekly workers) is enterprise-scale. Bullhorn Middle Office — configurable pay/bill rules including rate-card checks, quote-only pricing, an ATS-locked incumbent and pre-bill only, not post-remittance. HighRadius / Versapay / Billtrust — deduction and cash-application suites built for CPG-style trade deductions, enterprise priced, with no staffing/VMS rate-card logic. RevRecovery (revrecovery.org) — generic AI contract-to-invoice leak scan across SaaS/MSP/staffing at $499–$3,999/mo plus 25% of recovery, but testimonials are self-described early access and traction is unverified. Gradient MSP Synthesize (~$199/mo) — the same shape of product in the MSP vertical, reconciling vendor seat counts to PSA agreements; notably it does quantities, not contract rates or escalators, which is the gap being described here. The open gap: nobody credible is selling a self-serve, post-remittance, contract-truth audit to sub-$100M staffing suppliers at a price they will sign without a procurement cycle.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. ASA-cited figures put ~26,000 US staffing and recruiting enterprises in existence, ~57% in temp/contract; SIA's published list only counts the 214 firms above $100M, so the $10M–$100M band is not publicly sized — call it low thousands of firms as an estimate. A $40M contract staffing firm at 22% gross margin carries ~$8.8M of gross profit; recovering even 0.5% of billings is $200k. That supports $1.5k–$5k/month SaaS plus a contingency share, comparable to RevRecovery's published $499–$3,999/month monitoring tiers and 25%-of-recovery fee, and well under the $50k–$150k/yr third-party estimates for HighRadius/Versapay deduction suites. Realistic first-year target: 20–40 firms at ~$30k ACV.
risks: 1) Data access: rate cards live in email and signed PDFs, remittances arrive as portal downloads or consolidated PDFs, and the VMS may not expose an API to the supplier — the first version may depend on forwarded files, which caps automation. 2) Dispute recovery may be politically unattractive: account managers at staffing firms protect the client relationship and may suppress small disputes rather than file them, turning a found dollar into an unclaimed one. 3) Hercules.ai already does the contract-vs-invoice check and is well funded; if it moves downmarket with a self-serve tier the gap narrows fast. 4) The headline numbers (5% of billable revenue, rate card drift examples) are all vendor- or association-published; the real recoverable amount per firm is unproven until the first free audit runs.
riskiest_assumptions: Most fragile first: (1) that a real staffing firm's past 90 days of remittances actually contain recoverable underpayments at a rate worth paying for — if a free audit on three firms turns up under ~0.2% of billings, the business is not there; (2) that the controller, not the account manager, controls the decision to dispute, and will actually file the claims the tool generates; (3) that rate cards, amendments and remittances can be obtained as files from the supplier side without VMS cooperation, repeatably enough to run weekly.
first_customers: The first 10: US contract staffing firms with $10M–$80M revenue and heavy VMS exposure — IT staffing shops in Dallas/Atlanta/Edison NJ, light-industrial firms in the Midwest, and allied-health staffing firms. Find them via (a) SIA's "fastest-growing staffing firms" and state staffing association member lists (NJSA, Illinois Search and Staffing, CSP); (b) LinkedIn search for titles "Billing Manager / Director of Back Office / Controller" at companies tagged Staffing & Recruiting with 50–500 employees; (c) the Bullhorn and Avionté partner/marketplace ecosystems and their user conferences (Bullhorn Engage, Avionté Nexus); (d) funding-partner networks (Advance Partners, Madison Resources) whose staffing clients already outsource back office and whose field reps see the billing mess firsthand.
validation_test: This week: offer a free "90-Day Short-Pay Audit" to 15 staffing controllers found on LinkedIn and at one state staffing-association chapter. Ask for three things only: their client rate cards (PDF), 90 days of VMS remittance advices, and the matching invoice register export. Run the reconciliation by hand plus a model, and return a one-page list of underpaid lines with dollar amounts and the contractual dispute deadline on each. Pass signal: at least 4 of 15 send files within 10 days, and at least 2 of those audits surface ≥0.3% of audited billings in defensible underpayments, with at least one controller saying "file these for me." Fail signal: firms refuse to share remittances, or the audits come back clean — which would mean the VMS pays correctly and the thesis is wrong.
build_plan: Stack: TypeScript + Next.js, Postgres, a document-parsing pipeline on Claude/GPT with structured output, S3 for files, and a scheduled agent (the builder's UiPath Maestro background maps cleanly to the orchestration + email-handling parts). Narrowest first version, sold as a paid audit before it is a product: (1) Rate-card extractor — ingest executed client agreements, amendments and rate-card attachments; emit a versioned, effective-dated rate table per client/role/location with OT multiplier, shift differential, escalation clause and program-fee percentage. (2) Remittance parser — ingest VMS remittance advices and invoice register exports (CSV/PDF) and normalise to invoice-line level. (3) The variance engine — join the two, classify each line as paid-correct, underpaid-rate, missing-premium, missed-escalation, over-deducted-fee, or timing; show expected vs paid vs variance with the source clause quoted. (4) Dispute pack — generate the written dispute email per client with the contract clause, the lines, the totals, and the notice deadline computed from the agreement; the controller clicks send. (5) Weekly re-run with a one-screen "money found this week" digest. Cut from v1: no VMS API integrations (files only), no ERP write-back, no collections chasing, no pay-side/payroll audit, no pre-bill prevention — post-remittance recovery only, because that is where the found-money proof lives.
launch_post: Your VMS doesn't pay what your contract says. Shortpay reads your signed rate cards and every remittance line, finds the missed escalations, dropped OT multipliers and over-deducted program fees — and writes the dispute before the 30-day window closes. Free 90-day audit.
reasoning: Tonight's bookmarks were mostly developer-tool noise; the live thread was the Grok Bot accounting post — an order-to-cash back office run by agents, with company-reported numbers (invoicing 24h → minutes, cash recon 3–4h → 30 min, ~8 hours/day freed). The temptation was to build the agent-governance layer around that, but the library already holds Shiftlog and the screen found OpenAI, Microsoft, ServiceNow and Atomicwork all there. The more interesting read is the one step the Grok Bots explicitly flag to a human and do not solve: short payments. That is where the generic "revenue leakage" category collapses — everyone checks the invoice against the contract; almost nobody checks the *payment* against the contract. Staffing suppliers in MSP/VMS programs are the sharpest instance: the client's VMS, not the supplier, computes the bill rate, so a stale rate table or a missed escalation silently takes 1–4 points off a 22% gross margin, and many supplier agreements waive disputes not raised in writing within a fixed window. The buyer is named and has a budget (they employ billing clerks at ~$50k and already buy middle-office software); the pain is expressed (SIA published >5% of billable revenue to preventable billing errors; Teambridge publishes worked clawback and drift examples; r/msp shows the same shape of complaint in the adjacent vertical). The pick builds on no past idea's buyer: Escalator served trade contractors on their own outbound contracts, Shortfall served insurance agencies on carrier commission statements — Shortpay serves staffing controllers on VMS remittances, a different buyer, a different document set and a post-payment rather than pre-invoice wedge. It is not a 9 because the gap is only 7: Hercules.ai genuinely performs contract-vs-invoice validation for staffing and is funded, and every leakage percentage I found is vendor- or association-published rather than measured. The free 90-day audit is the cheap way to find out whether the money is real.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Shortpay — post-remittance contract-vs-payment audit agent for staffing suppliers in VMS programs. PICK: named buyer with a budget line, recurring weekly pain, a deadline mechanic, and the incumbents either stop at the invoice (Monk) or sell enterprise managed services (Hercules).
2. Agent onboarding/evidence layer for finance bots (from the Grok Bot post) — dropped at screen: too close to past idea Shiftlog, and the screen found OpenAI Frontier, Microsoft Agent 365, ServiceNow Control Tower and Atomicwork all occupying agent governance.
3. MSP CSP-to-PSA billing reconciliation (Pax8/Partner Center vs ConnectWise agreements) — finalist, lost: Gradient MSP Synthesize sells exactly this from $199/mo and r/msp threads show many MSPs already automated the seat-count half. Reshaped the contract-rate/escalator half into Shortpay's logic instead.
4. Contract escalator enforcement for mid-market B2B services generally — finalist, lost: too horizontal, and this buyer overlaps the library's Escalator idea; research showed xfactrs/Dimely/RevRecovery already crowd the generic version.
5. Implementation-partner UAT/config tooling off the Auctor post — dropped at screen: repeats Signoff and Asbuilt in the library, and Auctor itself just raised a $20M Sequoia Series A for the adjacent workflow.
6. "Plaid for government benefits" document-proof wedge (YC RFS, Alströmer) — dropped at screen: 12–24 month public-sector sales cycle, wrong fit for an evenings-and-weekends builder with no agency relationships.
7. AI plan-review correction-letter tooling for city building departments (YC "AI for City Hall") — dropped at screen: overlaps the library's Backcheck, and the buyer is a municipality with a procurement cycle, not a weeks-to-first-sale wedge.
8. Facilities-services (janitorial/security/landscaping) unbilled extra-work capture — dropped at screen: research found only a vendor-claimed 5–8% leakage figure and no credible buyer complaints; WinTeam and Janitorial Manager already own the workflow, and the library already has Escalator in this vertical.
9. Meeting-artifact governance after Claude Meetings (who generated what doc, in which call, with whose consent) — dropped at screen: repeats Bouncer's buyer and workflow, and it is a feature Anthropic will likely ship itself.
10. Remote agent control plane / approve-from-phone for self-hosted agents (KlausCodes question + DigitalOcean Cuttlefish) — dropped at screen: DigitalOcean just shipped it free with Managed Agents, and the buyer is a developer with no budget line.
11. Deduction root-cause for services suppliers outside staffing (logistics, agencies) — dropped at screen: HighRadius and Versapay own deduction management at $50k–$150k/yr estimates, and the non-staffing versions lack the VMS rate-card mechanic that makes Shortpay findable.

PROJECT
1. Shiftboard — type your job, get a night shift staffed from 1,142 real public Grok Bots + the tasks nobody built yet. PICK: live growing dataset nobody has presented personally, open-CORS JSON, rides a 3-day-old 11k-like post.
2. Bot Bouncer — paste a Grok Bot share link, get a blast-radius score before you copy it. Dropped at deep research: SafetyCard, killerskills.ai, agent-blast-radius and two community "Template Safety Checker" bots already occupy this, and x.ai share pages likely block browser fetch (no CORS) so it can't run static.
3. Composewatch — paste docker-compose.yml, see what breaks on Apple container 1.7.1 incl. the new k8s cluster support. Dropped at screen: straight repeat of past idea Defect.
4. Clusterkit — Apple container k8s cluster config generator for Mac devs. Dropped at screen: tiny audience, nothing to post, and `mocker` already covers the compose gap.
5. Blastdoor-for-Actions — paste a repo URL, see every workflow and bot that can write to it. Dropped at screen: GHA Scanner's web UI already does paste-a-public-repo, zizmor has an online version, and Perplexity confirmed the unauthenticated API can't actually answer "who can push".
6. Laundryclock — the "it's been N days since" tracker from the location-reminder post. Dropped at screen: thousands of free versions, no new capability, nothing to share.
7. Untangle Report — paste a repo, get a messy-code scorecard. Dropped at generate: thin variation on a named project in the bookmarks (/untangle-codebase) and adjacent to past ideas Blindspot/Ghostwritten.
8. Meeting Artifact Gallery — public gallery of what Claude Meetings produces. Dropped at reading: confirmed no public API or webhook for Claude Meetings artifacts, so there is no dataset to present.
9. Liveapp Shelf — a browsable shelf of apps people shipped with Cursor Live Apps. Dropped at reading: Perplexity confirmed there is no public directory or feed of Cursor live apps, so the dataset does not exist.
10. Delegability — your week's tasks scored against the Agent Delegability Index paper. Dropped at screen: near-repeat of past ideas Bottleneck and Roster (same O*NET-task-scoring workflow, same audience).
11. SIP Friction — visualising how many steps Indian mutual-fund onboarding takes. Dropped at generate: no dataset, regulated subject, wrong audience for this builder.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised x.ai/news/grok-bot-accounting (five bots across order-to-cash, three-week onboarding, 24h→minutes invoicing, 3–4h→30min cash recon — this is what pushed me toward the O2C back office rather than agent governance); Auctor (confirmed $20M Sequoia Series A Apr 2026 and that it sells to implementation partners, which killed candidate 5 as both a repeat and a funded incumbent); DigitalOcean Cuttlefish (free app, usage-billed Managed Agents — killed candidate 10). Screening pot (6/6): AR/O2C agent landscape (HighRadius, Versapay, Fazeshift, Concourse); "AI coworker" agent governance (found OpenAI Frontier, Atomicwork, Microsoft Agent 365, ServiceNow, Zafin, Concourse — killed candidate 2); Claude Meetings competitive noise (killed 9); city-permit search returned nothing usable (candidate 7 dropped on sales-cycle grounds); revenue-leakage statistics (EY-cited 1–5% of EBITA, widely repeated); contract-to-billing vendor map (xfactrs, Dimely, RevRecovery, Quivly — showed the horizontal version is crowded, killing candidate 4). Deep research pot (12/12): RevRecovery pricing and credibility ($499–$3,999/mo, 25% of recovery, early-access testimonials only); MSP CSP-to-PSA reconciliation incl. Gradient Synthesize pricing (~$199/mo) and 2024–2026 r/msp threads (killed candidate 3, but revealed that Synthesize does quantities not rates/escalators — the insight that reshaped the pick); staffing VMS billing reconciliation and leakage numbers; Monk funding and scope ($25M Series A Apr 2026, >$1B receivables managed, portal submission + collections + short-pay flagging); Hercules.ai Bill scope and funding (~$26M Series B 2024, pre-bill contract checks, enterprise managed service, Ōnin Group); facilities-services unbilled extras (weak evidence, killed candidate 8); CLM coverage of obligation-to-billing (Sirion closest, all enterprise-priced, none doing revenue-side escalator-to-invoice checks for sub-$100M firms); staffing back-office cost benchmarks (billing clerk ~$49.8k); staffing market sizing (SIA only counts 214 firms ≥$100M; ASA-cited ~26,000 enterprises; 20–25% contract gross margin); Reddit first-person search (thin — logged as a weakness). Sharpening pot (5/5): Teambridge rate-card drift and clawback worked examples; SIA "Revenue Leakage: The Silent Threat to Staffing Firm Margins" (>5% of billable revenue, 7–14 days DSO); remittance/deduction vendor check (confirmed Monk stops at invoice-level short-pay, HighRadius deduction suites are CPG-shaped and $50k–$150k/yr estimates); pre-bill audit feature check across Bullhorn Middle Office, Avionté, CEIPAL (Bullhorn is the only confirmed rate-card check, quote-only, pre-bill); dispute time-bar research (found a public contract requiring written dispute notice within 30 days of invoice date or waiver — this became the product's urgency mechanic and lifted the wedge). Investor signals weighed: YC "The $15-an-Hour Expert" and a16z "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" both support the pick's capability claim; YC "AI for City Hall" and "Plaid for Government Benefits" were considered and dropped on sales-cycle and builder-fit grounds; a16z "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" shaped the free-audit go-to-market rather than the product.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.8): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6 before). The original candidate was a generic "contract-to-billing revenue leakage auditor for mid-market B2B". Research showed that space is genuinely crowded and vague: xfactrs, Dimely, RevRecovery, Botminds, plus CLM vendors all claim contract-vs-invoice checks, and none of them has a defensible wedge. Change to the idea: pick one vertical where the money is lost on the *payment* side rather than the invoice side — staffing suppliers in MSP/VMS programs — and move the wedge from pre-bill to post-remittance. Research found this holds: Teambridge documents rate-card drift and clawbacks with worked examples (37% of an assignment's gross margin on a $2/hr retroactive cut; 22% contracted vs 18.5% realised margin on a 200-contractor book), SIA published that preventable billing errors cost staffing firms >5% of billable revenue and add 7–14 days DSO, and the one well-funded contract-check product (Hercules.ai Bill) is an enterprise managed service with no public price showcasing an 18,000-worker customer. Gap 6 → 7 (not higher: Hercules genuinely does the check and could move downmarket). Pain 7 → 8 on the SIA and Teambridge numbers plus r/msp-style first-person underbilling threads. Round 2 — weak criterion: wedge (7 before). Change: make the first sellable unit a free 90-day short-pay audit delivered from files the supplier already has (rate card PDFs + remittance advices), with a contingency share, rather than an integrated product. Research found supplier agreements can waive undisputed amounts after a fixed window — one public contract requires written notice within 30 days of invoice date — which gives the audit a deadline-driven hook and means the first deliverable (a dispute pack with a countdown) is sellable before any integration exists. Wedge 7 → 8. Timing lifted 7 → 8 on the confirmed Monk Series A (Apr 2026) and the SpaceXSI Grok Bot order-to-cash publication, both inside the last year. Average 7.2 → 7.8.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): Perplexity on apple/container 1.7.1 cluster.md (confirmed experimental local k8s, released 6 Nov 2026 — killed two candidates as too niche/repeat); on Claude Meetings (confirmed NO public API or webhook for artifacts — killed the gallery idea outright); on x.ai/news/grok-bot-accounting (got the five named roles — Provisioning, Billing, Billing Support, Cash Applications, Collections — which became the "night shift" framing). A fourth summary on Cursor Live Apps came from the screening pot and confirmed no public app directory exists.
Screening pot (5/5): searches for remote-agent control dashboards (crowded: goose, Symphony, Kilo), untangle-codebase (no results, thin), Claude Code transcript cards (near past idea Payslip), GitHub Actions workflow auditors (found GHA Scanner's paste-a-URL web UI and zizmor's online version — killed candidate 5), and "days since" trackers (saturated — killed candidate 6).
Deep research pot (8/8), all on the Grok Bot corpus: confirmed the Marketplace and community directories exist and their counts (GrokShelf 185 verified from 113 creators across 11 categories; grokbotshelf 1,142–1,144); confirmed public share pages expose identity, description, skills and routines but are not a security boundary; confirmed Grok Bot's approval model (Auto Review, Ask-first rules, gated actions) which told me what "needs access to" can honestly claim; confirmed O*NET 31.0 is CC BY but that the O*NET route was a repeat of past ideas; and crucially established that grokbotshelf.com ships bots.json plus /api/search with Access-Control-Allow-Origin:* — that single fact moved the build from "needs a scraper and a backend" to "static page", and is why buildability is 9. It also found the competing security-card tools that killed candidate 2.
Sharpening pot (4/4): two calls established the growth/diff mechanic (bots.json field list, `added` dates, category filter, no documented search rate limit, and the confirmed caveat that `connectors`/`routines` are optional creator-supplied fields — which is why the spec shows "needs:" as best-effort and the build plan says degrade gracefully); two calls tested the reframed hook, finding that job→bot-team matching exists only as paid in-product Team Builder/Task Router bots and that the task-by-task coverage view across public shared bots is the open gap. Net effect of research: one candidate survived contact, two were killed by missing datasets, two by existing free tools, three by past-idea collision.
Sharpening (7.8 to 8.4): Round 1 — weakest criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: you read your roster once and leave). Change to the idea: added the weekly diff. The catalogue is growing fast (GrokShelf: 185 verified bots on 16 Nov from a smaller base; Grok Bot Shelf: 1,142 in docs vs 1,144 on the homepage on 24 Nov — the count visibly moves), so a saved roster plus a Monday re-snapshot gives a real "3 new bots now cover your week" message rather than a fake streak. Research (Perplexity on grokbotshelf): bots.json is a full public catalogue with an `added` date field and an open-CORS /api/search, so weekly diffs are trivially computable and the source is stable enough to snapshot. Usefulness 5 → 7 (capped below 8: I could not verify how many genuinely new bots land per week, only that counts move). Buildability 8 → 9 on the same evidence (open CORS + static JSON = no backend beyond one key-holding function).

Round 2 — weakest remaining: wow (7, "a list of bots" is a plain result). Change to the idea: the headline output became the negative space — "nobody has built this yet", with copy-paste starter instructions — and the roster was reframed as a staffed night shift with times, mirroring the SpaceXSI five-bot team the bookmark describes. Research (Perplexity on prior art for job→bot-team matching) found Team Builder / Team Hub / Task Router bots and xAI's own manager-bot guide all build rosters from scratch inside a paid Grok plan, and explicitly concluded that task-by-task matching and a coverage view across public shared bots is the undemonstrated gap — which is exactly the uncovered-task view. Wow 7 → 8; freshness held at 9 (corpus and trigger are weeks old, confirmed, but not released this week). Shareability 8 → 9: the card is built to be posted and the "5 of 7 of my job" format is the shape of thing that has spread before; not raised to 10 because I found no verified viral comparable for agent-related score cards.
prototype_summary: An interactive Shortpay prototype that turns 90 days of staffing remittance lines into a ranked, clause-cited list of $11,842.90 in recoverable short-pays with dispute deadlines and a ready-to-send dispute pack.
